newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa 1997 GDP growth seen unchanged at 3.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa 1997 GDP growth seen unchanged at 3.1 pct.

text.p: The University of Stellenbosch's Bureau for Economic Research said it expected real GDP growth of 3.1 percent in 1997, unchanged from 1996 but down on its previous forecast of 3.6 percent.

In an update of his economic review, economist Pieter Laubscher said capital expenditure to boost exports and several large construction projects could counterbalance otherwise slowing economic conditions.
"We argued previously that even domestic demand conditions could recover meaningfully in the second half of 1997, but have scaled this forecast down somewhat," he said.
"Net exports are likely to be the main stimulant for renewed growth in the second half of the year."

He said the economy was clearly in a downward phase of the business cycle in the fourth quarter of 1996, with low levels of confidence in the retail and wholesale sectors as trading conditions tightened.
The slowdown in manufacturing was more widely dispersed, although the deterioration seemed to be stabilising.
In the building and construction sectors, conditions deteriorated in the fourth quarter and the outlook for the next year was less promising.
Laubscher said it was likely that sluggish domestic demand would continue in the first two to three quarters in 1997.
An export led recovery was expected in the second half of the year because of better world economic prospects and the more competitive rand exchange rate.
"We are likely to have underestimated the real export growth for 1996, which could (including gold) be around 8.5 percent compared to our forecast of six percent," he said.
On the import side, pre-emptive purchases of durable goods, machinery and equipment as well as inventory stockpiling delayed the impact of the weaker rand.

Higher import costs and slower growth in domestic spending curtailed import growth in the fourth quarter and Laubscher estimated a seasonally adjusted surplus of 500 million rand on the current account of the balance of payments.

"This is unlikely to signify a more permanent change to a surplus on the current account, but we have scaled our previous forecast of a 9.4 billion rand deficit for 1997 down to 6.2 billion rand," he said.
He estimated a deficit for the 1996 calendar year of between nine and 10 billion rand.
Because of unexpected increases in food prices, Laubscher said he had revised his forecast of consumer price inflation in 1997 upwards to 8.9 percent from 8.2 percent.
He expected inflation to fall during the second half of the year, mainly for technical reasons and the expected lowering of interest rates in the second half of the year.
Real growth in private consumption spending was now expected to be slightly below two percent compared to the previously forecast 2.6 percent.
